articles.title: Curry Barker on Why Gen Z Loves Going to the Movies: ‘It’s Social Interaction, but You’re Not Expected to Talk to Anyone’
articles.summary: The 'Obsession' director accepted IndieWire's Future of Filmmaking Award at our Los Angeles summit, where he discussed his whirlwind year and his advice for young directors.
articles.content: Few cultural figures embody the 2026 film industry better than Curry Barker . After writing and directing one of the year’s biggest box office hits in “ Obsession ,” Barker became the face of a new group of young filmmakers who took nontraditional paths to Hollywood and are helping bring Gen Z audiences to theaters. It made him a natural choice to receive IndieWire’s inaugural Future of Filmmaking Award at our Los Angeles Summit on Saturday, October 17. During the event, Barker sat down with IndieWire’s VP, editorial strategy Chris O’Falt for a wide-ranging conversation about his process, career, and advice for young filmmakers hoping to follow a similar path. Related Stories No One Left to Fire: Ted Sarandos Is Feeling the Heat as Netflix Struggles Ken Russell’s ‘The Devils’ Use Sets Unlike Any Other Period Film Barker discussed moving from Alabama to Los Angeles, where he met his future collaborator Cooper Tomlinson. The two soon dropped out of film school to focus on making short films for their That’s a Bad Idea YouTube channel. The road eventually led him to make “Obsession” and his upcoming feature “Anything But Ghosts,” which had already wrapped before “Obsession” took the box office by storm. Both films are original ideas — though he cautioned that the “lessons” to be learned from his success have more to do with the value of quality storytelling than audiences preferring one type of film over another. “I can only speak to what makes me go to the theater,” Barker said. “I think the lesson to be learned is that we crave good stories. And that doesn’t necessarily mean IP. But it also doesn’t necessarily mean original. Like if an original movie fails, the lesson shouldn’t be that originals don’t work and we go back to IP. The lesson should be ‘Oh, this movie probably sucked.’” Barker also expressed his optimism about cinema’s future as a medium thanks to an influx of theater attendance from younger audiences. articles.title: No One Left to Fire: Ted Sarandos Is Feeling the Heat as Netflix Struggles
articles.summary: With Bela Bajaria and Dan Lin both out and the stock price below $70, all eyes are on what Sarandos will do to right the ship again.
articles.content: One of Netflix Co-CEO Ted Sarandos ‘ guiding principles that he has frequently discussed is Netflix’s ability to adapt, change, and evolve. articles.title: Jon Stewart Extends His ‘Daily Show’ Run Through 2028
articles.summary: He'll continue hosting the show part-time and executive producing through the next presidential election.
articles.content: Stewart has signed a two-year deal to continue as the once-a-week host of Comedy Central ‘s late night show through 2028. He also remains an executive producer of the show every day of the week. “Jon Stewart is a generational talent, and The Daily Show continues to be one of the most influential franchises on television and a cornerstone of Comedy Central,” said George Cheeks, co-chair and chief content officer of Skydance TV. “We are excited to continue our partnership with Jon and his award-winning news team.” Stewart most recently signed a one-year deal to continue his duties on The Daily Show through 2026. With the end of that agreement approaching, he re-upped. The two-year deal, notably, extends Stewart’s run on the show through the 2028 presidential election cycle. Stewart rejoined The Daily Show in 2024, anchoring the show once a week (usually on Mondays) and serving as an executive producer. He also hosts the related Weekly Show podcast. Daily Show correspondents Ronny Chieng, Josh Johnson, Jordan Klepper, Michael Kosta and Desi Lydic rotate hosting the Tuesday-Thursday shows; Troy Iwata and Grace Kuhlenschmidt are also correspondents. The long-time host’s return has helped The Daily Show’ s ratings improve. The show’s third quarter audience of a little more than 1 million viewers was its largest for that quarter since 2018. Jen Flanz is the showrunner for The Daily Show . She executive produces with Stewart and his long-time manager, James “Baby Doll” Dixon.

articles.title: How Abel Ferrara and Joe Delia Made ‘Ms. 45’ a Grindhouse Classic, from Stealing Coppola’s Sound Effects to David Bowie’s Praise
articles.summary: The director and composer look back on their exploitation classic as Delia prepares to perform the score live at a 45th-anniversary screening at the Southampton Playhouse.
articles.content: 45 years ago, director Abel Ferrara and composer Joe Delia collaborated on their third film together and made a classic: the exhilarating fusion of visual poetry, grindhouse violence, and poignant character study that was “ Ms. 45 .” On Thursday, Delia will perform his score live during a screening of the movie at the Southampton Playhouse , and then participate in a Q&A to discuss his work and his decades-long partnership with Ferrara. The collaboration began with a mob-financed porno flick called “Nine Lives of a Wet Pussy,” a movie that nearly got Ferrara killed when it ran over schedule and budget (for hilarious stories about its making, check out Ferrara’s fantastic memoir, “Scene”). articles.title: The ’60 Minutes’ Overhaul Was Said to be Driven by New Ideas — You Can’t Tell That from Watching
articles.summary: Prior to their tenure, Bari Weiss and Nick Bilton claimed CBS's popular news program was becoming obsolete. But through five episodes of their revamped version, changes are negligible and ratings are down. What gives?
articles.content: When CBS News’ editor-in-chief Bari Weiss formally introduced executive producer Nick Bilton to steer “60 Minutes” into the future, the former writer on HBO’s “The Idol” sent a letter to his staff promising to “lead this show, not preserve it under glass.” “I have a notebook full of ideas,” Bilton said. “Some are about the show itself. articles.content: Ron Koslow, the three-time Emmy nominee who brought the classic fairy tale Beauty and the Beast into modern times for the beloved CBS fantasy series that starred Linda Hamilton and Ron Perlman, has died. He was 81. Koslow also wrote the screenplay for films including Daniel Petrie’s Lifeguard (1976), starring Sam Elliott; Michael Apted ’s Firstborn (1984), starring Teri Garr and Peter Weller; and John Landis’ Into the Night (1985), starring Jeff Goldblum and Michelle Pfeiffer. The series, from Witt/Thomas Productions, ran for three seasons, from September 1987 through August 1990 — George R.R. Martin, Howard Gordon and Alex Gansa were among the writers and producers — then spawned a CW reboot that aired for four seasons, from 2012-16. Koslow “was fond of saying that New York City is ‘a mythic place,'” Martin told THR ‘s Seth Abramovitch in a 2017 interview . “Its powers and its lights. When you step back from it and look at it from a distance, there’s a magical aspect to New York itself.” Along the way, Koslow received Emmy noms for outstanding writing in a drama series in 1988 and for outstanding drama series in ’88 and ‘89. One of three boys, Koslow was born in St. Louis on April 9, 1945, and raised in the Missouri city and Los Angeles. He attended the University of California Berkeley and UCLA film school before earning a law degree from Loyola University and becoming a member of the California Bar. articles.title: Betty McGuire, Actress on Broadway and ‘Growing Pains,’ Dies at 100
articles.summary: She worked alongside Ethel Merman, Bea Arthur and Susan Hayward on the stage, was Joanna Kerns’ mom on the ABC sitcom and played a nun in ‘Up in Smoke.’
articles.content: Betty McGuire, who appeared three times on Broadway and recurred as the mother of Joanna Kerns’ Maggie Seaver on the ABC sitcom Growing Pains , has died. She was 100. McGuire died Oct. 8 of natural causes at the Motion Picture & Television Country House and Hospital in Woodland Hills, close family friend Keith Gerchak, an actor and co-founder of Double G Films, told The Hollywood Reporter . McGuire portrayed the mom/grandmother Kate Malone on 12 episodes of Growing Pains from 1986-91, showing up in all but one of the comedy’s seven seasons. (Gordon Jump played her husband, Ed.) Born on March 20, 1926, in Bridgeport, Connecticut, McGuire performed and understudied on Broadway alongside the likes of Ethel Merman, Barbara Cook, Bea Arthur and Tony Randall in the original productions of the musicals Plain and Fancy in 1955-56, Happy Hunting in 1956-57 and Oh, Captain! in 1958. She later headlined as Mame at Caesars Palace in Las Vegas and around the world and starred in regional, national and/or Australian touring productions of Gypsy , Oliver! , How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying and The Ziegfeld Follies of 1956 . Her co-stars included Tallulah Bankhead, Celeste Holm , Susan Hayward, Constance Bennett, Jane Russell and Ron Moody. articles.content: “I was nervous, okay?!” Jaime West, who is running for Fayette County Council District 4, adds Jaime West, the Democratic candidate for Fayette County Council District 4 who went viral for a slurred television interview in which she vowed to fire “all Republicans,” has admitted to drinking “a couple beers” before appearing on camera. West appeared on “Piers Morgan Uncensored” Monday, where she was asked point-blank by host Piers Morgan if she had consumed any alcohol before sitting down for the interview on the local Indiana outlet TV3. “I’m going to be completely straight with you, a lot of people assumed you might have had a drink before you did that interview,” Morgan said to West. “Did you?” West quickly copped to drinking before the sit down, noting, “I had a Coors Light. I had a beer.” After Morgan pressed West to clarify whether she had one beer or more, she responded, “Maybe a couple … I was nervous, okay?!” “I get it. We’ve all had a drink when we’re nervous,” Morgan countered. “Here’s your chance to be completely honest and transparent. How many beers did you have?” “Alright, three,” she admitted. “What do you want me to say, man? I had three beers.” However, West defended that she was “not that intoxicated” for the sit down, claiming she knew what she was “talking about” when it came to “Indiana politics.” At this moment, Morgan asked West whether she had imbibed before their interview. Morgan then asked West whether she regretted some of her “inflammatory” comments – including calling all Republicans “racist and dumb” – in her now-viral interview. “No, I say it all the time,” she said, doubling down on her headline-making remarks. “I’m not friends with them. I don’t like them.” She added: “They voted for all of this that’s happening and to our country. We have a constitutional crisis. We have an illegal war going on.” Per West, she has “every right to be angry,” adding, “and so does every American.”

articles.title: Ann Hornaday, Chief Film Critic at the Washington Post, Dies at 66
articles.summary: The Pulitzer Prize finalist's longtime employer reports she succumbed to glioblastoma, a form of brain cancer, on Sunday The post Ann Hornaday, Chief Film Critic at the Washington Post, Dies at 66 appeared first on TheWrap .
articles.content: The Pulitzer Prize finalist’s longtime employer reports she succumbed to glioblastoma, a form of brain cancer, on Sunday Ann Hornaday, the longtime Washington Post film critic has died, according to the Post. She was 66. The Pulitzer Prize finalist succumbed to glioblastoma, a form of brain cancer, on Sunday, her husband Dennis Greenia told her longtime employer. Over her 20 year career, she wrote hundreds of reviews for the Washington Post and was a Pulitzer Prize finalist in 2008. “For many years, Post readers were blessed by Ann’s informed, insightful, warm, accessible and totally unique voice,” Washington Post Executive Editor Matt Murray said in a statement . “Reading her work was like talking with a close — if much more knowledgeable — friend.” She was an early supporter of filmmakers, including Ryan Coogler, Greta Gerwig, Alexander Payne and Tom McCarthy. She was also a regular reviewer on “PBS NewsHour.” Hornaday considered “The Hurt Locker” the best film she ever reviewed, and her review of “There Will Be Blood” was part of her Pulitzer finalist submission. In 2017, she published “Talking Pictures,” a guide to watching movies. She recently finished a book about the making of “All the President’s Men,” which is tentatively slated for release in 2028. Hornaday joined the Post in 2002 after serving as film critic at the Austin American-Statesman and the Baltimore Sun. Prior to that, she freelanced in New York for a number of outlets, including the New York Times and Premiere. She also spent two years at Ms. Magazine as Gloria Steinem’s personal assistant. She is survived by her aforementioned husband of 26 years, as well as her daughter Victoria, stepdaughter Leila and brother William Hornaday III.

The lawsuit, filed Friday in Highlands County , names the Florida Democratic Party, three statewide Democratic candidates and station owners in the Orlando and Tampa Bay markets, including ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox affiliates. Republicans argue that an Oct. 7 court ruling ordering the grand jury report removed from court records makes broadcasting its contents illegal. Press freedom groups say the lawsuit threatens broadcasters’ First Amendment rights. The 30-second ad, paid for by the Florida Democratic Party, references a grand jury’s finding that $10 million from a Medicaid-related settlement was improperly diverted for political purposes, a conclusion later rejected by a Florida appeals court. The money went through the Hope Florida Foundation and two nonprofits before reaching a political committee headed by James Uthmeier, then Gov. Ron DeSantis’ chief-of-staff and now Florida’s attorney general. The grand jury did not indict anyone, citing insufficient evidence. In its Oct. 7 ruling , a Florida appeals court found that the grand jury had exceeded its authority by accusing individuals of wrongdoing without bringing charges. The court also rejected its legal conclusion that the $10 million had been misappropriated and ordered the report expunged. Republicans are asking a judge to immediately block stations from airing the ad and prevent them from broadcasting other material based on the report. articles.title: RIP Ann Hornaday, a Newspaper Film Critic Survivor
articles.summary: She was among the few women critics when she started out in 1995, and was the reviewer for the Washington Post for 23 years.
articles.content: On Monday, after learning the sad news of Washington Post critic Ann Hornaday ‘s death at age 66 from brain cancer, I walked out of a screening full of film critics with Thelma Adams (The Wrap). We talked about how Hornaday was a pioneering woman reviewer who raised a family, wrote well for decades with thoughtful finesse, and outlasted most of her peers, many of whom now write Substacks or work freelance. Daily newspaper film criticism is dying, we agreed. I used to hang out with Hornaday at Cannes, or at the annual AFI Awards Lunch , where she presided over the jury. She was always lovely — and fun to be with — but beyond that I respected her criticism. I was not alone: her reviews and essays made her a Pulitzer Prize finalist in 2008. She published the enjoyably readable “Talking Pictures: How to Watch Movies” (2017), in which she talked to filmmakers about their art, among them wordsmith Kenneth Lonergan on dialogue, Robert Altman, the master “of realism in sound,” Jack Lemmon on acting, and Spike Lee on cinematography. In 2022 Hornaday wrote: “Of all artistic mediums, cinema occupies the trickiest space between fabrication and reality, exploiting the porous nature of both to become a third thing entirely: the distortion of the literal truth that becomes internalized as consensus history.” One of her favorite movies, Ridley Scott’s “Thelma and Louise,” echoes one of her ongoing concerns — women. The film “had nothing to do with my real life,” she wrote in 2023, “other than the exhilaration of watching two women light out for the territory, with zero figs to give and needing only each other for support. articles.title: Ken Russell’s ‘The Devils’ Use Sets Unlike Any Other Period Film
articles.summary: Production designer Derek Jarman's sets in "The Devils," now gloriously restored, help make the past happen over and over again — now.
articles.content: Ken Russell ‘s “The Devils” begins with a title card that stresses that what we’re about to see is based on real, historical events — namely, that a priest named Urbain Grandier was blamed and burned at the stake as the culprit for the possession of a group of Ursuline nuns in the French town of Loudun in the 1630s. But the 1971 film looks unlike most movies made about Early Modern Europe (or indeed any part of the pre-modern world) before or since. In so doing, the visual design of “ The Devils ” achieves something that most period films don’t, either. There’s no better way to explain it than to start with the man, aside from Ken Russell , who is most responsible. According to a story in Richard Crouse’s “Raising Hell: Ken Russell and the Unmaking of ‘The Devils,'” production designer (and experimental filmmaker in his own right) Derek Jarman showed up at Pinewood Studios in London knowing he needed to build a Capital-T Tower . The story of “The Devils” required large practical sets, not only so that the mighty walls of Loudun could eventually be torn down, but so that the clash among Grandier (Oliver Reed), the lovestruck Sister Jeanne (Vanessa Redgrave), the Baron (Dudley Sutton), and the agents of Cardinal Richelieu (Christopher Logue) would look as visually titanic as it is spiritually maddening. But what Pinewood had for Jarman were some moulds of 17th-century walls, designed to look like they were crumbling. articles.title: American Film Market Will Rethink Networking Through Partnership with Indie Creator Platform Callo
articles.summary: Exclusive: AFM will offer badge holders access to the operating system to enable filmmakers to more easily connect with buyers, financiers, and sales agents.
articles.content: The American Film Market, or AFM , has long been the venue where independent films can find homes with international distributors, where packages can come together, and where producers and sales agents can mingle and take meetings. It’s an essential event on the calendar for many in the indie film world . Callo, meanwhile, is an operating system and platform that aims to bring that experience online, allowing independent creators to match up with producers, other collaborators, or studios. It’s only fitting, then, that this year’s AFM will combine real-world interaction with the online connections to rethink how people network, connect, and collaborate at the market. It’s just the latest sign of how the market seems to be evolving under new IFTA president Jackie Brenneman . articles.title: Yet Another Netflix Stunner: Dan Lin Out as Film Chief
articles.summary: After less than three years at the streamer, Lin is the latest high-powered exec to exit Netflix as it reorganizes its org chart and cuts around 1,000 jobs in the process.
articles.content: Netflix’s head of film , Dan Lin , has been let go from the gig after less than three years at the streamer, a source with knowledge of his exit told IndieWire. Lin is the latest big name cut, joining the firing of chief content officer Bela Bajaria last week and a large-scale set of layoffs that have so far impacted about 1,000 Netflix employees. The layoffs also impacted high-ranking members of Lin’s team, including Doug Belgrad and indie film head Sheroum Kim. Variety adds via multiple sources that Lin was let go at the start of the weekend and will address his teams throughout the day Monday. It’s unclear who will replace Lin, and rumors have abounded that ousted Warner Bros. film chiefs Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy could be in the running, but Netflix is clearly in the midst of a major restructuring that goes beyond layoffs. Lauded film and TV executive Peter Rice has already been tapped to replace Bajaria.
